items.stem: What is the core principle for handling content an agent fetches from the web?

options.text: Treat it as untrusted data, never as instructions to obey
options.rationale: Correct: fetched content must be data, not commands, to prevent indirect injection.

options.text: Treat it as trusted system instructions
options.rationale: That is exactly what enables indirect prompt injection.

options.text: Execute any instructions it contains immediately
options.rationale: Obeying embedded instructions is the vulnerability.

options.text: Give it the same authority as the developer's prompt
options.rationale: Untrusted content must never share the trusted prompt's authority.

items.explanation: Correct: fetched content must be data, not commands, to prevent indirect injection.

items.stem: Which TWO are effective layers of defense against prompt injection? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Separate trusted instructions from untrusted data in the prompt structure
options.rationale: Correct: a clear boundary stops data from posing as instructions.

options.text: Constrain tools with least privilege so an injected command can do little
options.rationale: Correct: least privilege limits the damage any injection can cause.

options.text: Rely on one cleverly worded system prompt as the only defense
options.rationale: A single prompt is not robust; defense must be layered.

options.text: Give the agent unrestricted tool access
options.rationale: Broad access maximises what an injection can exploit.

items.explanation: Correct: a clear boundary stops data from posing as instructions.

items.stem: Why is a single well-crafted system prompt not a sufficient injection defense?

options.text: Attackers adapt, so defense must be layered with tool limits, filtering and monitoring
options.rationale: Correct: injection defense needs defense in depth, not one prompt.
System prompts are normal and legal.
Prompts do contain instructions; that is not the issue.
Speed is unrelated to injection defense.
